cards.name: Afghanistan
cards.story: Unified in 1747 under Ahmad Shah Durrani, Afghanistan's modern borders—including its narrow northeastern Wakhan Corridor—were largely drawn during the 19th-century 'Great Game' rivalry between the British and Russian empires. Afghanistan won full diplomatic independence from Britain in 1919.
cards.contestedNote: The 1893 Durand Line separating Afghanistan and Pakistan divides ethnic Pashtun communities and has long been politically sensitive.

cards.name: Albania
cards.story: After nearly five centuries under Ottoman rule, Albania declared independence in 1912. Major European powers drew its modern borders at the 1913 London Conference, leaving many ethnic Albanians in neighboring lands.

cards.name: Algeria
cards.story: Conquered by France beginning in 1830 and expanded deep into the Sahara by French colonial administrators, Algeria fought an eight-year war of independence. The 1962 Évian Accords ended colonial rule and established Africa's largest country by land area.

cards.name: Andorra
cards.story: Tucked high in the Pyrenees mountains, Andorra kept its borders through a 1278 agreement sharing leadership between the Bishop of Urgell in Spain and a French count (later the President of France). That medieval treaty still shapes its unique sovereignty today.

cards.name: Angola
cards.story: Portuguese traders arrived on Angola's coast in the late 1400s, and European treaties in the 1880s drew its inland borders across historic kingdoms like Kongo and Ndongo—including the coastal exclave of Cabinda. Angola won independence in 1975 after a long liberation struggle.

cards.name: Antigua & Barbuda
cards.story: British colonists settled Antigua in 1632 and linked nearby Barbuda under one colonial administration in 1860. The twin-island nation gained full independence from the United Kingdom in 1981.

cards.name: Argentina
cards.story: Argentina broke free from the Spanish Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1816. Military expansion into Indigenous Patagonian lands and an 1881 Andes boundary treaty with Chile established its sweeping southern borders.

cards.name: Armenia
cards.story: With roots stretching back over 2,500 years in the Caucasus highlands, Armenia briefly formed an independent republic in 1918 before becoming a Soviet republic in 1920. Its modern borders became international lines when the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
cards.contestedNote: Armenia and Azerbaijan are engaged in ongoing talks to formally demarcate parts of their shared border following decades of conflict.

cards.name: Australia
cards.story: Home to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples for over 60,000 years, the continent was divided into six separate British colonies in the 18th and 19th centuries. Those six colonies united in 1901 to form the Commonwealth of Australia.

cards.name: Austria
cards.story: Once the heart of the vast Austro-Hungarian Empire, Austria shrank to its modern German-speaking borders after World War I. Following World War II and Allied occupation, the 1955 Austrian State Treaty restored it as a neutral republic.

cards.name: Azerbaijan
cards.story: After a brief republic in 1918–20, Azerbaijan was incorporated into the Soviet Union with borders including the western exclave of Nakhchivan. It regained independence when the USSR collapsed in 1991.
cards.contestedNote: Nagorno-Karabakh was the focus of decades of conflict with Armenia before Azerbaijan reestablished full control over the internationally recognized region in 2023; border demarcation talks continue.

cards.name: Bahamas
cards.story: Home originally to the Lucayan people, the Bahamas archipelago became a British crown colony in 1718 after decades as a pirate haven. Its 700 islands and cays achieved peaceful independence in 1973.

cards.name: Bahrain
cards.story: An ancient Persian Gulf trading archipelago ruled by the Al Khalifa family since 1783, Bahrain entered a British protection treaty in the 1800s. When Britain withdrew from the Gulf in 1971, Bahrain chose separate independence rather than joining the UAE.

cards.name: Bangladesh
cards.story: The 1947 Partition of British India split historic Bengal, making its eastern half 'East Pakistan'—separated from West Pakistan by 1,000 miles of India. After a devastating 1971 war of independence, it emerged as the sovereign nation of Bangladesh.

cards.name: Barbados
cards.story: Unlike many Caribbean islands that changed European rulers repeatedly, Barbados stayed continuously under British colonial control from 1627 until 1966. It gained independence peacefully and became a parliamentary republic in 2021.

cards.name: Belarus
cards.story: Belarus's western borders were reshaped during World War II when Soviet territory expanded westward into former eastern Poland. When the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, those internal republic boundaries became the borders of independent Belarus.

cards.name: Belgium
cards.story: Belgium broke away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands in the 1830 revolution. The 1839 Treaty of London finalized its modern borders and established it as a bridge between French- and Dutch-speaking regions.

cards.name: Belize
cards.story: Built around British timber settlements on the Caribbean coast of Central America, Belize was known as British Honduras until 1973. It achieved independence in 1981, though neighboring Guatemala long disputed part of its southern border.
cards.contestedNote: Guatemala and Belize agreed to submit their long-standing border claim to the International Court of Justice for peaceful settlement.

cards.name: Benin
cards.story: Built around the powerful West African Kingdom of Dahomey and northern savanna societies, French colonial borders stretched north from a narrow Atlantic coastline to the Niger River. Independent since 1960, the nation renamed itself Benin in 1975.

cards.name: Bhutan
cards.story: Never colonized by a European empire, Bhutan was unified in the 1600s and shaped its southern border with British India through an 1865 treaty. The modern monarchy began in 1907, preserving its Himalayan independence ever since.

cards.name: Bolivia
cards.story: Named for liberator Simón Bolívar in 1825, Bolivia originally stretched all the way to the Pacific Ocean. It lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–84) and southeastern plains in the 1930s Chaco War, leaving it landlocked.

cards.name: Bosnia & Herzegovina
cards.story: Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence in 1992 during the breakup of Yugoslavia, sparking a devastating three-year war. The 1995 Dayton Accords ended the fighting and preserved its outer borders while dividing governance into two internal entities.
cards.contestedNote: Its external borders are internationally recognized, though internal political divisions established by the Dayton Accords remain deeply sensitive.

cards.name: Botswana
cards.story: In 1885, Tswana chiefs sought British protection as the Bechuanaland Protectorate to prevent annexation by neighboring settler territories. It achieved peaceful independence as Botswana in 1966 along those protectorate boundaries.

cards.name: Brazil
cards.story: Unlike Spanish South America, which split into many republics, Portuguese Brazil stayed united after declaring independence in 1822. Skilled diplomacy and the 1903 Treaty of Petrópolis (acquiring Acre from Bolivia) completed South America's largest country.

cards.name: Brunei
cards.story: Once a mighty maritime sultanate covering much of Borneo, Brunei shrank during the 1800s as surrounding lands became Sarawak under British influence—splitting Brunei into two small coastal enclaves. It regained full independence from British protection in 1984.

cards.name: Bulgaria
cards.story: Bulgaria won autonomy from the Ottoman Empire in 1878 and full independence in 1908. Its boundaries shifted through the Balkan Wars and World Wars before settling into their modern lines in 1940.

cards.name: Burkina Faso
cards.story: France carved out the colony of Upper Volta in 1919 across the Mossi kingdoms and neighboring peoples, temporarily broke it apart, and restored its borders in 1947. Independent since 1960, it adopted the name Burkina Faso ('Land of Upright People') in 1984.

cards.name: Burundi
cards.story: Unlike many African borders drawn from scratch, Burundi closely follows a centuries-old highland kingdom that predated European arrival. Colonized first by Germany and then administered by Belgium after World War I, Burundi regained independence in 1962.

cards.name: Cambodia
cards.story: Heir to the great medieval Khmer Empire of Angkor, Cambodia became a French protectorate in 1863, during which French treaties with Siam (Thailand) returned the Angkor region to Cambodian borders. Cambodia achieved independence from France in 1953.

cards.name: Cameroon
cards.story: Originally colonized by Germany as Kamerun, the territory was split between France and Britain after World War I. French Cameroon gained independence in 1960, and the southern half of British Cameroons voted in 1961 to reunite with it, shaping its distinctive triangle.

cards.name: Canada
cards.story: Canada began in 1867 when four British North American provinces united in Confederation across Indigenous homelands. Treaties, land purchases, and provinces joining over the next 82 years—ending with Newfoundland in 1949—created its coast-to-coast borders.

cards.name: Cape Verde
cards.story: Uninhabited until Portuguese navigators landed in the 1450s, the ten volcanic islands of Cabo Verde became a major Atlantic hub during the transatlantic slave trade. Following Portugal's 1974 revolution, the archipelago gained independence in 1975.

cards.name: Central African Republic
cards.story: France carved out the colony of Ubangi-Shari in the late 1800s as part of French Equatorial Africa, drawing straight-line borders across dozens of communities. The territory gained independence in 1960 as the Central African Republic.

cards.name: Chad
cards.story: French colonial conquest around Lake Chad joined Saharan nomadic regions in the north with savanna farming societies in the south. Chad became independent along those French administrative lines in 1960, and the International Court of Justice confirmed its northern Aouzou border with Libya in 1994.

cards.name: Chile
cards.story: Wedged between the Andes and the Pacific, Chile won independence from Spain in 1818. Victory in the War of the Pacific extended its northern desert border, while treaties with Argentina and Peru fixed its remarkable 2,600-mile length.

cards.name: China
cards.story: China's modern borders largely inherit the vast multi-ethnic territory consolidated under the Qing Dynasty (1644–1912), transitioning through the 1912 Republic and the 1949 founding of the People's Republic of China, with Hong Kong and Macau returning in 1997 and 1999.
cards.contestedNote: China has active territorial disputes over Taiwan, sections of its Himalayan border with India, and maritime boundaries in the South China Sea.

cards.name: Colombia
cards.turningPoint: 1831 Dissolution of Gran Colombia & 1903 Panama Exit
cards.story: After independence from Spain, Colombia anchored Simón Bolívar's dream union of Gran Colombia alongside Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panama. Venezuela and Ecuador departed in 1830, and Panama broke away in 1903, leaving Colombia's modern borders.

cards.name: Comoros
cards.story: Lying in the Mozambique Channel between Madagascar and mainland Africa, the Comoros islands were colonized by France in the 1800s. Three of the four main islands declared independence in 1975, while Mayotte voted to remain part of France.
cards.contestedNote: Comoros claims the fourth island of the archipelago, Mayotte, which voted to become an overseas department of France.

cards.name: Costa Rica
cards.story: After breaking free from Spain in 1821, Costa Rica joined the short-lived Federal Republic of Central America. When that union dissolved in 1838, Costa Rica became an independent nation, settling its borders with Nicaragua and Panama through later treaties.

cards.name: Côte d'Ivoire
cards.story: Named by European sailors for its coastal ivory trade, France turned the region into a colony in 1893 and drew straight eastern and northern boundaries with neighboring British and French territories. Côte d'Ivoire gained independence in 1960.

cards.name: Croatia
cards.story: Shaped like a crescent along the Adriatic coast, Croatia's outline grew from historic kingdoms within the Habsburg and Venetian worlds. Its modern borders became international lines when it declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.

cards.name: Cuba
cards.story: Cuba fought decades of rebellions to end nearly four centuries of Spanish colonial rule. Following U.S. intervention in 1898, Cuba became a formal republic in 1902, though the U.S. retained a leased naval base at Guantánamo Bay.

cards.name: Cyprus
cards.story: Cyprus gained independence from Britain in 1960 under a power-sharing agreement between Greek and Turkish Cypriots. Following a 1974 coup and Turkish military intervention, a UN buffer zone divided the island across Nicosia.
cards.contestedNote: The Republic of Cyprus is internationally recognized across the whole island, while the northern third is administered separately as Northern Cyprus (recognized only by Turkey).

cards.name: Czech Republic
cards.story: After the fall of Austria-Hungary in 1918, Czechs and Slovaks united to form Czechoslovakia. Following the end of Communist rule, both parliaments voted to split peacefully in 1993, creating the modern Czech Republic along historic Bohemian and Moravian lines.

cards.name: Denmark
cards.story: One of Europe's oldest continuous kingdoms, Denmark once ruled much of Scandinavia. Its modern southern border with Germany was settled peacefully in 1920 when local residents voted by referendum on which country to join.

cards.name: Djibouti
cards.story: Sitting at the strategic entrance to the Red Sea, France established French Somaliland in the late 1800s as a coaling port and railway hub to Ethiopia. Following an independence vote, Djibouti became a sovereign republic in 1977.

cards.name: Dominica
cards.story: Long defended by the Indigenous Kalinago people against European settlement, mountainous Dominica passed between France and Britain before becoming a British colony. It gained independence directly as a republic in 1978.

cards.name: Dominican Republic
cards.story: Colonial treaties split the island of Hispaniola between French Haiti in the west and Spanish Santo Domingo in the east. After twenty-two years of unified rule under Haiti, the eastern two-thirds declared independence in 1844 as the Dominican Republic.

cards.name: DR Congo
cards.story: At the 1885 Berlin Conference, King Leopold II of Belgium claimed the vast Congo basin as a personal colony—later taken over by Belgium in 1908—leaving a narrow corridor to the Atlantic Ocean. The Democratic Republic of the Congo won independence in 1960.

cards.name: East Timor
cards.story: Colonial treaties split the island of Timor between the Dutch west (later Indonesia) and the Portuguese east. After Portugal withdrew in 1975, Indonesia occupied the territory for 24 years until Timorese voters chose independence in a 1999 UN referendum—forming Timor-Leste in 2002.

cards.name: Ecuador
cards.story: Ecuador became an independent republic in 1830 upon leaving Gran Colombia, and claimed the Galápagos Islands two years later. Long-running Amazon border disputes with Peru were finally resolved peacefully by treaty in 1998.

cards.name: Egypt
cards.story: Anchored by the Nile River for over five millennia, Egypt's straight desert borders were set during Ottoman and British rule in the early 1900s. Following wars in the Sinai Peninsula, Israel returned the Sinai to Egypt by 1982 under the 1979 peace treaty.

cards.name: El Salvador
cards.story: El Salvador gained independence from Spain in 1821 and served as the final stronghold of the Federal Republic of Central America. When the federation collapsed in 1841, it became Central America's smallest mainland nation.

cards.name: Equatorial Guinea
cards.story: Portugal traded the Gulf of Guinea island of Bioko and nearby mainland rights to Spain in 1778. Joined together as Spanish Guinea, the mainland strip of Río Muni and offshore islands gained independence as Equatorial Guinea in 1968.

cards.name: Eritrea
cards.story: Italy carved Eritrea along the Red Sea coast as a colony in 1890 before it was federated with—and later annexed by—Ethiopia after World War II. Following a thirty-year struggle, Eritreans voted overwhelmingly in a 1993 UN-supervised referendum for independence.

cards.name: Estonia
cards.story: Estonia first declared independence from the Russian Empire in 1918, before being annexed by the Soviet Union during World War II. During the peaceful Singing Revolution in 1991, Estonia restored its independence along its current borders.

cards.name: Eswatini
cards.story: Built around the Swazi Kingdom consolidated in the 1800s, the territory became a British protectorate in 1903 after losing surrounding grazing lands to colonial neighbors. Independent since 1968, Swaziland officially updated its name to Eswatini in 2018.

cards.name: Ethiopia
cards.story: One of the world's oldest continuous nations, Ethiopia defeated Italian invasion at Adwa in 1896 and was never formally colonized (aside from a brief World War II occupation). When Eritrea voted for independence in 1993, Ethiopia became landlocked along its modern borders.

cards.name: Fiji
cards.story: Chiefly kingdoms across the Fijian islands unified under Ratu Seru Epenisa Cakobau before ceding sovereignty to Britain in 1874. Almost a century later, Fiji's more than 300 islands achieved peaceful independence in 1970.

cards.name: Finland
cards.story: After centuries under Swedish and then Russian rule, Finland declared independence in 1917 during the Russian Revolution. Its eastern border shifted west after World War II treaties ceded Karelia and Petsamo to the Soviet Union.

cards.name: France
cards.story: France's familiar hexagon formed over centuries as medieval kingdoms unified under Paris. Its modern eastern border with Germany settled after World War I when Alsace-Lorraine returned to France, alongside overseas territories kept from its colonial era.

cards.name: French Guiana
cards.story: Colonized by France in the 1600s, French Guiana sits on South America's northeastern coast between Suriname and Brazil. Rather than becoming independent, it voted in 1946 to become an integral overseas department of France and part of the European Union.
cards.contestedNote: French Guiana is not a sovereign country, but a full overseas region of France governed under French and EU law.

cards.name: Gabon
cards.story: French explorers signed coastal treaties in the 1840s and expanded into the rainforest interior as part of French Equatorial Africa. Gabon achieved independence along those colonial boundaries in 1960.

cards.name: Gambia
cards.story: The Gambia's remarkably narrow, winding shape traces the Gambia River, surrounded on three sides by Senegal. An 1889 agreement between Britain and France gave Britain roughly six miles on each side of the river, forming the borders of independent Gambia in 1965.

cards.name: Georgia
cards.story: Situated between the Black Sea and the Caucasus Mountains, ancient Georgian kingdoms came under Russian imperial rule in the 1800s and Soviet rule in 1921. Georgia declared restored independence in April 1991 as the USSR dissolved.
cards.contestedNote: Abkhazia and South Ossetia are internationally recognized as part of Georgia, though both operate as Russian-backed breakaway regions.

cards.name: Germany
cards.story: Germany first unified from dozens of kingdoms and duchies in 1871, then shrank and was split into West and East Germany after World War II. When the Berlin Wall fell, the two halves reunited in 1990 and formally confirmed the Oder-Neisse border with Poland.

cards.name: Ghana
cards.story: Combining the British Gold Coast colony, the Ashanti Kingdom, northern territories, and a UN trust strip of Togoland that voted to join, Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence in 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah.

cards.name: Greece
cards.story: Modern Greece won independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1830 as a much smaller state in the south. Over the next century, wars and treaties added northern regions and Aegean islands, finishing with the Dodecanese islands from Italy in 1947.

cards.name: Grenada
cards.story: Known as the Spice Isle, Grenada shifted from French to British colonial rule in 1763 after the Seven Years' War. Together with the smaller islands of Carriacou and Petite Martinique, it gained independence from Britain in 1974.

cards.name: Guatemala
cards.story: Once the heart of Maya civilization and later Spain's administrative center for Central America, Guatemala broke from Spain in 1821. After leaving the Central American Federation in 1839, treaties with Mexico finalized its northern borders in 1882.

cards.name: Guinea
cards.story: Part of French West Africa since the 1890s, Guinea was the only colony to vote 'No' to remaining in a French-led community in 1958. Choosing immediate sovereignty, it became independent along its colonial borders that October.

cards.name: Guinea-Bissau
cards.story: Carved out on West Africa's coast by an 1886 border agreement between Portugal and France, Portuguese Guinea waged a determined independence war led by Amílcar Cabral's movement. Portugal formally recognized Guinea-Bissau's independence in 1974.

cards.name: Guyana
cards.story: Originally settled by the Dutch and later ceded to Britain as British Guiana in 1814, Guyana is South America's only English-speaking nation. It won independence in 1966, though Venezuela continues to claim the western Essequibo region.
cards.contestedNote: Guyana administers the Essequibo region under an 1899 arbitration award, which Venezuela disputes.

cards.name: Haiti
cards.story: In the world's only successful nationwide slave revolt, formerly enslaved people overthrew French colonial rule in Saint-Domingue. In 1804, Haiti became the first independent Black republic and the second independent country in the Americas.

cards.name: Honduras
cards.story: After independence from Spain in 1821, Honduras belonged to the Federal Republic of Central America until leaving the union in 1838. Britain later returned the Bay Islands and Mosquito Coast to Honduras, completing its modern borders.

cards.name: Hungary
cards.story: After Austria-Hungary collapsed at the end of World War I, the 1920 Treaty of Trianon redrew Central Europe along new national borders. Hungary lost roughly two-thirds of its former kingdom's territory, creating its compact modern outline.

cards.name: Iceland
cards.story: Settled by Norse and Celtic voyagers over a thousand years ago, Iceland spent centuries under Norwegian and Danish rule. When Denmark was occupied during World War II, Icelanders voted overwhelmingly in 1944 to become a fully independent island republic.

cards.name: India
cards.story: After nearly two centuries of British rule and a massive independence movement, British India was partitioned in August 1947 into independent India and Pakistan, displacing millions. Over 560 princely states integrated into India to form its modern map.
cards.contestedNote: India's northern borders include long-running disputes with Pakistan over Kashmir and with China along the Line of Actual Control.

cards.name: Indonesia
cards.story: Stretching across more than 17,000 islands, Indonesia inherited the vast archipelago of the Dutch East Indies after declaring independence in 1945 and winning Dutch recognition in 1949. Western New Guinea (Papua) was incorporated in the 1960s, while East Timor later voted for independence.

cards.name: Iran
cards.story: Inheriting thousands of years of Persian statehood, Iran was never formally colonized by Europe. Its modern borders were narrowed in the 1800s through treaties with the Russian Empire in the north and British India in the east.

cards.name: Iraq
cards.story: After the Ottoman Empire fell in World War I, Britain merged three distinct Ottoman provinces—Mosul, Baghdad, and Basra—into a single League of Nations mandate across Mesopotamia. Iraq became formally independent in 1932.

cards.name: Ireland
cards.story: After centuries of British rule and a war of independence, the 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty partitioned the island. Twenty-six southern counties formed what became the Republic of Ireland, while six northern counties remained part of the United Kingdom.

cards.name: Israel
cards.story: Following the end of the British Mandate of Palestine and the 1947 UN Partition Plan, Israel declared independence in May 1948. The 1949 armistice agreements ('Green Line') set its initial borders, while the 1967 war brought the West Bank, Gaza, and Golan Heights under Israeli control.
cards.contestedNote: Israel's borders with Palestine (the West Bank and Gaza), Jerusalem's status, and the Golan Heights remain internationally disputed.

cards.name: Italy
cards.story: Known as the Risorgimento, the 1861 unification merged rival Italian kingdoms, duchies, and city-states into one nation. World War I and World War II peace treaties adjusted its northeastern Alpine and Adriatic borders into their modern form.

cards.name: Jamaica
cards.story: Originally inhabited by the Taíno people, Jamaica was colonized by Spain in 1509 and seized by Britain in 1655. After briefly joining the West Indies Federation, Jamaicans voted to leave and became fully independent in 1962.

cards.name: Japan
cards.turningPoint: 1951 San Francisco Treaty & 1972 Return of Okinawa
cards.story: Unified across its main islands for centuries, Japan expanded into an overseas empire in the late 1800s and early 1900s before losing those territories after World War II. Its modern archipelago borders were completed when the U.S. returned Okinawa in 1972.
cards.contestedNote: Japan and Russia still dispute four northern islands (the Southern Kurils / Northern Territories) held by Russia since 1945.

cards.name: Jordan
cards.story: Carved out east of the Jordan River from former Ottoman Syria under a British mandate in 1921, the Emirate of Transjordan gained full independence in 1946 as Jordan. A 1965 desert land swap with Saudi Arabia expanded its Red Sea coastline at Aqaba.

cards.name: Kazakhstan
cards.story: Spanning the vast Eurasian steppe once home to nomadic Kazakh khanates, Kazakhstan's borders were drawn as a Soviet republic in the 1920s and 1930s. In December 1991, it became the final republic to leave the Soviet Union, forming the world's largest landlocked nation.

cards.name: Kenya
cards.story: Britain and Germany divided East Africa across historic homelands in 1886—even bending the border around Mount Kilimanjaro—creating British East Africa. Following the Mau Mau uprising and constitutional talks, Kenya won independence in 1963.

cards.name: Kiribati
cards.story: Spanning all four hemispheres across the central Pacific, Kiribati was administered as the British Gilbert Islands colony. When the Ellice Islands split away to become Tuvalu, the remaining atolls became independent Kiribati in 1979.

cards.name: Kosovo
cards.story: Formerly an autonomous province within Yugoslavia and Serbia, Kosovo endured severe conflict in 1998–99 followed by UN administration. Its parliament declared independence in 2008 along its provincial boundaries.
cards.contestedNote: Kosovo is recognized as independent by over 100 countries, while Serbia and several other nations do not recognize its statehood.

cards.name: Kuwait
cards.story: Founded as a Gulf trading town in the 1700s, Kuwait became a British protectorate in 1899 to maintain autonomy from the Ottoman Empire. A 1922 British-brokered border treaty set its desert frontiers, and Kuwait gained full independence in 1961.

cards.name: Kyrgyzstan
cards.story: High in the Tian Shan mountains, Kyrgyz homelands were folded into the Russian Empire in the 1800s and given republic borders by Soviet planners in the 1920s–30s. Those internal borders became international lines when Kyrgyzstan declared independence in 1991.

cards.name: Laos
cards.story: Tracing its roots to the medieval Kingdom of Lan Xang, Laos took on its modern Mekong River borders in 1893 when France forced Siam (Thailand) to cede territory east of the river into French Indochina. Laos won full independence from France in 1953.

cards.name: Latvia
cards.story: Latvia proclaimed independence from imperial Russia in 1918 before being absorbed by the Soviet Union during World War II. As Soviet power waned in 1991, Latvia restored its sovereignty within its modern Baltic borders.

cards.name: Lebanon
cards.story: After the Ottoman Empire fell in World War I, France separated Mount Lebanon and neighboring coastal cities from Syria in 1920 to create Greater Lebanon. Lebanon gained full independence from France in 1943 along those mandate lines.

cards.name: Lesotho
cards.story: Founded by King Moshoeshoe I in the 1820s as a mountain refuge from regional wars, Basutoland sought British protection in 1868 to keep from being absorbed into surrounding South African territories. Completely enclosed by South Africa, it gained independence as Lesotho in 1966.

cards.name: Liberia
cards.story: Established in the 1820s by freed African Americans alongside diverse Indigenous coastal and interior peoples, Liberia declared independence in 1847—making it Africa's oldest modern republic. Border treaties with neighboring British and French colonies set its current outline.

cards.name: Libya
cards.story: Italy united three distinct Ottoman provinces—Tripolitania, Cyrenaica, and Fezzan—into the colony of Libya in 1934. After Italy's defeat in World War II, the United Nations oversaw Libya's transition to independence in 1951.

cards.name: Liechtenstein
cards.turningPoint: 1806 End of the Holy Roman Empire
cards.story: Formed when the Liechtenstein family united two small Alpine estates in 1719, this tiny principality became fully sovereign when Napoleon dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. Neutrality and close ties with Switzerland kept its borders unchanged ever since.

cards.name: Lithuania
cards.story: Once part of a vast medieval Grand Duchy, Lithuania regained independence in 1918 before Soviet annexation in 1940. In March 1990, it became the first Soviet republic to declare restored independence, keeping the Vilnius region within its modern borders.

cards.name: Luxembourg
cards.story: Luxembourg's modern borders were carved out by the 1839 Treaty of London, which gave its larger French-speaking western half to Belgium. An 1867 treaty then guaranteed the remaining Grand Duchy's independence and neutrality.

cards.name: Madagascar
cards.story: Settled over 1,500 years ago by seafarers from Borneo and East Africa, most of Madagascar was unified under the Merina Kingdom before French conquest in 1896. The world's fourth-largest island regained independence in 1960.

cards.name: Malawi
cards.story: Shaped tightly around the western shore of Lake Malawi, the British protectorate of Nyasaland was formed in 1891 after treaties with Portugal over southern Africa. It broke away from a colonial federation and became independent Malawi in 1964.

cards.name: Malaysia
cards.story: Malaya gained independence from Britain in 1957, then united in 1963 with Singapore and the Borneo states of Sabah and Sarawak to form Malaysia. When Singapore separated two years later in 1965, Malaysia took on its modern two-region shape.

cards.name: Maldives
cards.story: Made up of roughly 1,200 coral islands in the Indian Ocean, the Maldives remained an independent sultanate for centuries before becoming a British protectorate in 1887. The archipelago regained full sovereignty in 1965.

cards.name: Mali
cards.story: Home to the storied medieval empires of Ghana, Mali, and Songhai, the region was conquered by France as French Sudan in the late 1800s. After a brief union with Senegal dissolved, Mali became an independent republic in September 1960.

cards.name: Malta
cards.story: Positioned at the crossroads of the Mediterranean, Malta's islands were ruled by Phoenicians, Knights of St. John, France, and Britain. Malta gained peaceful independence from the British Empire in 1964 and became a republic in 1974.

cards.name: Marshall Islands
cards.story: Comprising 29 coral atolls in the central Pacific, the Marshall Islands passed from German and Japanese rule into the U.S.-run UN Trust Territory after World War II, enduring nuclear testing at Bikini Atoll. The islands gained independence in 1986.

cards.name: Mauritania
cards.story: Bridging Arab-Berber North Africa and West Africa across the Sahara, Mauritania's geometric desert borders were drawn by French colonial administrators in the early 1900s. It achieved full independence from France in 1960.

cards.name: Mauritius
cards.story: Uninhabited until Dutch, French, and later British settlers arrived in the Indian Ocean, Mauritius developed a deeply multicultural island society. It won independence from Britain in 1968, though the Chagos Islands' separation before independence remained disputed for decades.

cards.name: Mexico
cards.story: Mexico won independence from Spain in 1821 with a vast territory stretching into today's western United States. After Texas seceded and the 1846–48 U.S.–Mexico War ended, the Treaties of Guadalupe Hidalgo and the 1853 Gadsden Purchase set its modern northern border.

cards.name: Micronesia
cards.story: Ruled in turn by Spain, Germany, Japan, and a U.S.-administered UN Trust Territory after World War II, four island districts (Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, and Kosrae) chose to unite. They formed the independent Federated States of Micronesia in 1986.

cards.name: Moldova
cards.story: Moldova's borders largely follow the Soviet republic carved from historical Bessarabia and a strip east of the Dniester River in 1940. It became independent when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
cards.contestedNote: The eastern strip known as Transnistria has operated as a breakaway region since a 1992 conflict, though it is internationally recognized as part of Moldova.

cards.name: Monaco
cards.story: Ruled by the Grimaldi family since 1297, Monaco once controlled neighboring Riviera towns as well. Under the 1861 treaty with France, Monaco gave up those surrounding towns in exchange for formal French recognition of its compact coastal borders.

cards.name: Mongolia
cards.story: Once the launchpad of the vast 13th-century Mongol Empire, Outer Mongolia broke away as China's Qing Dynasty collapsed in 1911. Solidifying independence in 1921 with Soviet backing, it remained separate from Inner Mongolia inside China.

cards.name: Montenegro
cards.story: An independent mountain principality before joining Yugoslavia in 1918, Montenegro remained federated with Serbia after Yugoslavia broke up in the 1990s. In 2006, Montenegrins voted narrowly in a peaceful referendum to restore full independence.

cards.name: Morocco
cards.story: One of Africa's oldest continuous monarchies, Morocco was divided into French and Spanish protectorates in 1912 before regaining independence in 1956. Its southern boundary remains contested over Western Sahara.
cards.contestedNote: Morocco administers most of Western Sahara as its Southern Provinces, while the UN treats the territory's final status as unresolved.

cards.name: Mozambique
cards.story: Portugal held trading posts along the Indian Ocean coast from 1505 and negotiated Mozambique's long coastal borders with Britain during the 1890s Scramble for Africa. After a ten-year liberation war, Mozambique gained independence in 1975.

cards.name: Myanmar
cards.story: Britain conquered the Burmese kingdoms in three 19th-century wars and governed Burma alongside frontier hill regions as part of British India until 1937. Those central plains and ethnic borderlands gained independence together in 1948 as Burma (now Myanmar).

cards.name: Namibia
cards.story: Colonized by Germany in 1884—including the narrow Caprivi Strip acquired in 1890 to reach the Zambezi River—Namibia was ruled by South Africa for decades after World War I. Following a long freedom struggle and UN-monitored elections, it became independent in 1990.

cards.name: Nauru
cards.story: A single raised coral island rich in phosphate, Nauru was colonized by Germany in 1888 and later governed under an Australian-led UN trusteeship. Nauruans achieved independence in 1968, creating the world's smallest island nation.

cards.name: Nepal
cards.story: Unified from Himalayan hill kingdoms by Prithvi Narayan Shah in 1768, Nepal was never colonized by Britain. After the Anglo-Nepalese War, the 1816 Treaty of Sugauli set its modern east-west borders across the Himalayas.

cards.name: Netherlands
cards.turningPoint: 1648 Peace of Westphalia & 1839 Treaty of London
cards.story: The Dutch Republic won independence from Spain in 1648 after an eighty-year struggle. After a brief union with Belgium, the 1839 Treaty of London set its modern European borders—though Dutch engineers kept reshaping the coastline by reclaiming land from the sea.

cards.name: New Caledonia
cards.story: Annexed by France in 1853, New Caledonia is home to the Indigenous Kanak people alongside European and Pacific Islander communities. Under the 1998 Nouméa Accord, it governs itself with special autonomy inside France following three independence referendums.
cards.contestedNote: New Caledonia is a special collectivity of France; ongoing negotiations continue over its future constitutional status and Kanak self-determination.

cards.name: New Zealand
cards.story: Settled by Polynesian Māori navigators centuries ago, Aotearoa New Zealand entered British rule through the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi between the Crown and Māori chiefs. It transitioned peacefully into a self-governing dominion in 1907 and full sovereignty thereafter.

cards.name: Nicaragua
cards.story: Nicaragua withdrew from the Central American Federation in 1838 after earlier independence from Spain. Its modern Atlantic coastline was fully incorporated in 1894 when the formerly British-protected Miskito Coast joined the republic.

cards.name: Niger
cards.story: France and Britain drew Niger's southern boundary in the 1890s to separate French Sahara lands from British Nigeria, splitting historic Hausa communities across the line. Niger gained independence from France in August 1960.

cards.name: Nigeria
cards.story: Britain merged its separate Northern and Southern protectorates—home to hundreds of languages and great kingdoms like Benin, Oyo, and Sokoto—into a single colony in 1914. Nigeria won independence in 1960, with northern British Cameroons voting to join in 1961.

cards.name: North Korea
cards.story: Unified as a single kingdom for over a thousand years before Japanese colonial rule (1910–45), Korea was split at the 38th parallel by the USSR and the U.S. at the end of World War II. Two rival states formed in 1948, and the 1953 armistice fixed today's Demilitarized Zone.
cards.contestedNote: No formal peace treaty has replaced the 1953 armistice; both North and South Korea have historically claimed sovereignty over the entire peninsula.

cards.name: North Macedonia
cards.story: North Macedonia separated peacefully from Yugoslavia in 1991 along its existing republic borders. In 2019, it resolved a long-running naming dispute with Greece by adopting the name North Macedonia.

cards.name: Norway
cards.story: After centuries united first with Denmark and then with Sweden, Norway's parliament and citizens voted overwhelmingly in 1905 to end the union with Sweden peacefully. Its long mountain border with Sweden became one of Europe's calmest international frontiers.

cards.name: Oman
cards.story: One of the Arab world's oldest independent states, Oman built a famed Indian Ocean maritime empire stretching to Zanzibar before focusing back on Arabia. Treaties with neighbors in the late 20th century finalized its desert borders—including the northern Musandam exclave.

cards.name: Pakistan
cards.story: Created in August 1947 during the Partition of British India as a homeland for South Asian Muslims, Pakistan originally had two halves separated by India. After East Pakistan became independent Bangladesh in 1971, West Pakistan formed modern Pakistan.
cards.contestedNote: Pakistan and India have disputed the northern region of Kashmir since 1947, divided today along the Line of Control.

cards.name: Palau
cards.story: Part of the UN Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands after World War II, Palau chose not to join Micronesia in 1978 so it could chart its own course. It became fully independent in 1994, making it one of Oceania's youngest sovereign states.

cards.name: Palestine
cards.story: Following the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, Britain governed Palestine under a League of Nations mandate until 1948. After the 1948 war and the 1967 Six-Day War, Palestinian territories came to be defined around the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip.
cards.contestedNote: Recognized as a state by over 140 UN members and holding UN observer status, Palestine's final borders, sovereignty, and status remain at the center of an active, unresolved conflict.

cards.name: Panama
cards.story: For decades after Spanish rule ended, Panama was a northern province of Colombia. Backed by U.S. interest in building an interoceanic canal, Panama declared independence in 1903, and finally regained full control of the Panama Canal Zone in 1999.

cards.name: Papua New Guinea
cards.story: European powers sliced the vast island of New Guinea down the middle along the 141st meridian—the west went to the Netherlands, while the east was split between Britain and Germany. Australia combined the eastern halves after World War I and granted independence in 1975.

cards.name: Paraguay
cards.story: Paraguay declared independence from Spain in 1811 and lost vast territory to Brazil and Argentina in the catastrophic War of the Triple Alliance (1864–70). A 1938 treaty after the Chaco War with Bolivia confirmed its western Gran Chaco borders.

cards.name: Peru
cards.story: Center of the ancient Inca Empire and Spain's richest South American viceroyalty, Peru declared independence in 1821. Later border treaties with Chile, Brazil, Colombia, and Ecuador defined its modern coastal, Andean, and Amazonian territory.

cards.name: Philippines
cards.story: Spain linked over 7,000 islands into a single colony named for King Philip II starting in the 1560s, then ceded the archipelago to the United States in 1898 despite a Filipino independence revolution. Following World War II, the Philippines achieved full independence in 1946.

cards.name: Poland
cards.story: Erased from the map by neighboring empires in 1795, Poland was reborn in 1918 after World War I. Following World War II, Allied leaders at Potsdam shifted Poland's entire map roughly 150 miles west, losing eastern lands to the USSR while gaining former German territories.

cards.name: Portugal
cards.story: Portugal has some of the oldest unchanged land borders in the world. After pushing Moorish rulers south during the Reconquista, Portugal and Castile signed the 1297 Treaty of Alcañices, setting mainland boundaries that have barely moved in over 700 years.

cards.name: Qatar
cards.story: Jutting into the Persian Gulf, the Qatari peninsula came under the Al Thani family in the 1800s and signed a British protection treaty in 1916. When Britain ended its Gulf protectorates in 1971, Qatar became a fully independent state.

cards.name: Republic of the Congo
cards.story: At the 1884–85 Berlin Conference, European powers split the Congo River basin along the river itself—France claimed the northwestern bank as French Congo while Belgium took the vast interior opposite. French Congo became the Republic of the Congo in 1960.

cards.name: Romania
cards.story: Modern Romania began when the principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia united in 1859, then expanded dramatically in 1918 to include Transylvania. World War II treaties ceded northern Bukovina and Bessarabia to the USSR, locking in today's borders.

cards.name: Russia
cards.story: Expanding from the medieval Duchy of Moscow across Siberia to the Pacific, Russia became the core of the Russian Empire and later the Soviet Union. When the USSR dissolved in 1991, the Russian Soviet Republic's boundaries became the modern Russian Federation.
cards.contestedNote: Russia's internationally recognized 1991 borders do not include Ukrainian territories (such as Crimea) that Russia has claimed since 2014 and 2022.

cards.name: Rwanda
cards.story: Rooted in a centralized pre-colonial highland kingdom, Rwanda was colonized by Germany in the 1890s and transferred to Belgium after World War I. Following a 1959–61 social revolution, Rwanda gained full independence as a republic in 1962.

cards.name: Samoa
cards.story: An 1899 imperial treaty split the Samoan islands in two—the eastern islands became American Samoa, while the western islands went to Germany and later New Zealand administration. In 1962, Samoa became the first Pacific island nation to regain independence.

cards.name: San Marino
cards.story: Founded around 301 CE on Mount Titano, San Marino is often called the world's oldest surviving republic. Its hillside borders were last expanded in 1463, and Italy respected its independence during Italian unification in the 1860s.

cards.name: São Tomé & Príncipe
cards.story: First sighted by Portuguese navigators in the 1470s in the Gulf of Guinea, these two volcanic equatorial islands became early sugar and cocoa plantation colonies. They achieved independence from Portugal in 1975.

cards.name: Saudi Arabia
cards.story: Over three decades starting in 1902, Abdulaziz Ibn Saud united rival Arabian regions—including Najd and the Hejaz, home to Mecca and Medina—into one realm. He proclaimed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932, later formalizing desert borders with its neighbors.

cards.name: Senegal
cards.story: Dakar served as the capital of French West Africa while colonial borders wrapped around British-controlled Gambia along the Gambia River. Senegal gained independence in 1960—first briefly federated with Mali, then as its own republic that August.

cards.name: Serbia
cards.story: Serbia regained statehood from the Ottoman Empire in the 19th century and formed the center of Yugoslavia after World War I. After Yugoslavia fractured in the 1990s and Montenegro departed in 2006, Serbia became an independent republic again.
cards.contestedNote: Serbia considers Kosovo an autonomous southern province, whereas Kosovo declared independence in 2008 and is recognized by over 100 countries.

cards.name: Seychelles
cards.story: Scattered across 115 granite and coral islands in the Indian Ocean, Seychelles was settled by France in 1770 and ceded to Britain after the Napoleonic Wars in 1814. The archipelago achieved peaceful independence in 1976.

cards.name: Sierra Leone
cards.story: Freetown was founded in 1787 as a settlement for formerly enslaved people returning to West Africa, while Britain later added the surrounding inland chiefdoms as a protectorate in 1896. Both parts united into independent Sierra Leone in 1961.

cards.name: Singapore
cards.story: Developed by Britain as a key Asian trading port in 1819, the island of Singapore briefly joined the Federation of Malaysia in 1963 after colonial self-rule. Political and economic disagreements led to its peaceful separation in 1965, launching the modern island city-state.

cards.name: Slovakia
cards.story: Part of the Kingdom of Hungary for nearly a millennium, Slovak lands joined Czech lands in 1918 to create Czechoslovakia. In 1993, leaders of both halves negotiated a peaceful split, establishing Slovakia's modern borders.

cards.name: Slovenia
cards.story: Nestled between the Alps and the Adriatic Sea, Slovenia spent centuries inside the Habsburg Empire before joining Yugoslavia in 1918. It declared independence in June 1991 and secured its modern borders after a brief ten-day conflict.

cards.name: Solomon Islands
cards.story: Britain established a protectorate over the Solomon Islands in 1893 and later adjusted its northwestern boundary with German-held Papua New Guinea. After fierce World War II battles at Guadalcanal, the archipelago gained independence in 1978.

cards.name: Somalia
cards.story: During the Scramble for Africa, Somali-speaking lands were divided among Britain, Italy, France, and Ethiopia. In July 1960, British Somaliland and Italian Somaliland united upon independence to form the Somali Republic.
cards.contestedNote: Northern Somaliland has governed itself as a self-declared republic since 1991, though it remains internationally recognized as part of Somalia.

cards.name: South Africa
cards.story: Britain united four settler colonies—Cape, Natal, Transvaal, and Orange River—into the Union of South Africa in 1910 under white-minority rule. After decades of anti-apartheid struggle, 1994's multiracial elections reintegrated the apartheid-era 'homelands' into one democratic nation.

cards.name: South Korea
cards.story: After Japan's 1945 surrender ended thirty-five years of colonial occupation, Allied powers temporarily divided the Korean Peninsula into northern and southern zones. Following the devastating 1950–53 Korean War, the Demilitarized Zone became South Korea's heavily fortified northern border.
cards.contestedNote: The Demilitarized Zone separates South and North Korea under the 1953 armistice rather than a permanent peace treaty.

cards.name: South Sudan
cards.story: Britain administered northern and southern Sudan separately during colonial rule before merging them at independence in 1956, fueling decades of civil war. After a 2005 peace deal, nearly 99% of southern voters chose independence in 2011—creating the world's youngest country.
cards.contestedNote: Several border zones with Sudan, especially the oil-rich Abyei area, remain disputed and await final demarcation.

cards.name: Spain
cards.story: Modern Spain took shape when the kingdoms of Castile and Aragon united in 1469 and completed the conquest of Granada in 1492. The 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees fixed its mountain border with France, while Gibraltar remained a small British territory on its southern tip.

cards.name: Sri Lanka
cards.story: Ruled by ancient Sinhalese and Tamil kingdoms for millennia, the island saw Portuguese, Dutch, and finally British control across all of Ceylon by 1815. It gained peaceful independence in 1948 and adopted the name Sri Lanka in 1972.

cards.name: St. Kitts & Nevis
cards.story: St. Kitts was the site of the first permanent English and French colonies in the Caribbean in the 1620s. Paired with neighboring Nevis into a two-island federation, it became the smallest independent country in the Americas in 1983.

cards.name: St. Lucia
cards.story: St. Lucia changed hands between France and Britain fourteen times before Britain took permanent control in 1814. The Caribbean island gained full independence from the United Kingdom in 1979.

cards.name: St. Vincent & the Grenadines
cards.story: Defended fiercely by the Garifuna people well into the 1700s, St. Vincent and the northern Grenadine islands came under British colonial rule in 1783. The island chain became an independent nation in 1979.

cards.name: Sudan
cards.story: Ruled jointly by Britain and Egypt until gaining independence in 1956, Sudan was Africa's largest country for over half a century. When South Sudan voted peacefully to separate in 2011, Sudan took on its current borders along the Nile.
cards.contestedNote: Sudan's borders include ongoing territorial disputes with Egypt (the Hala'ib Triangle) and South Sudan (Abyei).

cards.name: Suriname
cards.story: Traded by England to the Netherlands in 1667 in exchange for New Amsterdam (modern New York), Suriname remained a Dutch colony for three centuries. It gained full peaceful independence in 1975.

cards.name: Sweden
cards.story: Once a major Baltic empire controlling Finland and lands across northern Europe, Sweden ceded Finland to Russia in 1809. After Norway's peaceful separation in 1905, Sweden maintained its modern Scandinavian borders in unbroken peace.

cards.name: Switzerland
cards.story: Born in 1291 as a mutual-defense pact among three Alpine valleys, Switzerland gradually grew into a confederation of 26 cantons. After Napoleon's defeat, the 1815 Congress of Vienna finalized Switzerland's modern borders and recognized its permanent neutrality.

cards.name: Syria
cards.story: Carved from Ottoman provinces after World War I under the Sykes-Picot framework, Syria was administered by France until winning full independence in 1946. Its southwestern Golan Heights border with Israel has remained contested since 1967.
cards.contestedNote: The Golan Heights has been under Israeli control since 1967, while most of the international community continues to consider it occupied Syrian territory.

cards.name: Taiwan
cards.story: Home to Indigenous Austronesian peoples before waves of Chinese settlement and fifty years of Japanese colonial rule (1895–1945), Taiwan became the seat of the Republic of China government in 1949 after the Chinese Civil War.
cards.contestedNote: Taiwan operates as a self-governing democracy, while Beijing considers it a province of China and most nations maintain unofficial ties.

cards.name: Tajikistan
cards.story: Nestled in the Pamir Mountains, Tajikistan's intricate borders—including winding valleys shared with Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan—were drawn by Soviet boundary commissions in the 1920s. It became an independent republic when the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991.

cards.name: Tanzania
cards.story: Mainland Tanganyika—once German East Africa, then a British UN trust territory—won independence in 1961, followed by the spice islands of Zanzibar in 1963. In April 1964, both merged into the United Republic of Tanzania, blending their two names.

cards.name: Thailand
cards.story: Known historically as Siam, Thailand is the only Southeast Asian country never colonized by a European power. To protect its core sovereignty as a buffer between British Burma and French Indochina, Siam ceded outer border provinces in treaties completed by 1909.

cards.name: Togo
cards.story: Originally the German colony of Togoland, the strip was split lengthwise between Britain and France after World War I. The western strip later voted to join Ghana, while French Togoland became the long, narrow Republic of Togo in 1960.

cards.name: Tonga
cards.story: Unified by King George Tupou I in 1845, Tonga is the only Pacific island nation never formally colonized by a foreign power. It entered a treaty of protection with Britain in 1900 to guard its sovereignty and resumed full foreign-policy independence in 1970.

cards.name: Trinidad & Tobago
cards.story: Britain combined the separate Caribbean colonies of Trinidad and Tobago into a single territory in 1889. Just off the coast of Venezuela, the twin-island nation gained independence from Britain in 1962.

cards.name: Tunisia
cards.story: Home to ancient Carthage and later a semi-autonomous Ottoman province, Tunisia became a French protectorate in 1881. A nationalist movement led by Habib Bourguiba won independence from France in 1956.

cards.name: Turkey
cards.story: When the centuries-old Ottoman Empire collapsed after World War I, Turkish nationalists led by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk rejected Allied partition plans and founded the modern Republic of Turkey in 1923. Spanning Asia and European Thrace, its final southern province (Hatay) joined in 1939.

cards.name: Turkmenistan
cards.story: Covering the vast Karakum Desert along the Caspian Sea, Turkmen lands were absorbed by Imperial Russia in the 1880s and shaped into a Soviet republic in 1924. Turkmenistan gained independence along those borders when the USSR dissolved in 1991.

cards.name: Tuvalu
cards.story: Formerly linked by Britain with the Micronesian Gilbert Islands, Polynesian islanders in the nine Ellice atolls voted in 1974 to separate peacefully. Four years later, they gained full independence as Tuvalu.

cards.name: Uganda
cards.story: Britain built the Uganda Protectorate around the powerful Kingdom of Buganda on Lake Victoria and linked neighboring kingdoms and northern communities under one border. Uganda gained independence from Britain in 1962.

cards.name: Ukraine
cards.story: Ukraine's modern boundaries took shape during the 20th century as western Ukrainian regions and Crimea were unified within the Ukrainian Soviet Republic. In December 1991, over 90% of voters backed full independence from the Soviet Union.
cards.contestedNote: Ukraine's 1991 borders—including Crimea and eastern regions—remain internationally recognized, though parts are currently under Russian military occupation.

cards.name: United Arab Emirates
cards.story: Long known as the Trucial States under British maritime treaties, six Persian Gulf emirates—led by Abu Dhabi and Dubai—chose to unite when Britain withdrew in December 1971. Ras Al Khaimah joined two months later, completing the seven-emirate federation.

cards.name: United Kingdom
cards.turningPoint: 1707 Union of Great Britain & 1922 Irish Partition
cards.story: England and Wales united in the 1500s, joined Scotland in 1707 to form Great Britain, and added Ireland in 1801. When most of Ireland became independent in 1922, the remaining union of Great Britain and Northern Ireland formed the modern United Kingdom.

cards.name: United States
cards.story: Starting as thirteen British colonies along the Atlantic coast in 1776, the United States expanded across Indigenous lands through treaties, wars, purchases like Louisiana (1803) and Alaska (1867), and the annexation of Hawaii. Alaska and Hawaii became the final two states in 1959.

cards.name: Uruguay
cards.story: Caught for decades between rival claims from Argentina and Brazil, the eastern bank of the Uruguay River was fought over repeatedly. British-mediated peace talks in 1828 resolved the war by recognizing Uruguay as an independent nation between both giants.

cards.name: Uzbekistan
cards.story: Home to legendary Silk Road cities like Samarkand and Bukhara, Uzbekistan's borders were drawn during the 1924 Soviet redrawing of Central Asia. It became an independent republic in 1991 and is one of only two doubly landlocked countries on Earth.

cards.name: Vanuatu
cards.story: Known colonially as the New Hebrides, this volcanic archipelago was unusually ruled jointly by both Britain and France from 1906 onward. Its islands united and achieved independence in 1980 as the Republic of Vanuatu.

cards.name: Vatican City
cards.story: For centuries, popes ruled wide Papal States across central Italy until Italian unification absorbed them in 1870. The 1929 Lateran Treaty with Italy created Vatican City as the world's smallest independent state inside Rome.

cards.name: Venezuela
cards.story: Venezuela was the first South American colony to declare independence from Spain in 1811, led by figures like Simón Bolívar. After separating from Gran Colombia in 1830, its modern borders emerged along the Caribbean coast and Orinoco basin.

cards.name: Vietnam
cards.story: With over a thousand years of historic kingdoms along the South China Sea, Vietnam fought French colonial rule until the 1954 Geneva Accords temporarily split it into North and South Vietnam. Following the Vietnam War, the country reunified in 1975.

cards.name: Western Sahara
cards.story: Colonized by Spain in 1884 with straight desert borders drawn by treaty with France, Spanish Sahara became disputed when Spain withdrew in 1975. Morocco moved to control most of the territory while the Sahrawi Polisario Front proclaimed an independent republic.
cards.contestedNote: The United Nations classifies Western Sahara as a non-self-governing territory whose final political status remains unresolved.

cards.name: Yemen
cards.story: Northern Yemen broke free from Ottoman rule in 1918, while southern Yemen and the port of Aden remained under British control until 1967. After decades as two separate Cold War states, North and South Yemen united in 1990 to form today's borders.

cards.name: Zambia
cards.story: Named for the Zambezi River, Zambia's butterfly-like outline was shaped when British colonial treaties with Belgium's Congo left the Katanga Pedicle jutting into its middle. Formerly Northern Rhodesia, it achieved independence in 1964.

cards.name: Zimbabwe
cards.story: Named for the medieval stone city of Great Zimbabwe, the region was colonized by Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company as Southern Rhodesia in the 1890s. Following a protracted liberation war against minority rule, Zimbabwe achieved recognized independence in 1980.
